text:
By the time Martin found the car, he had been arguing with his former wife for nearly four miles. She was not there. This was one of the improvements they had made to their marriage.

The argument concerned a blue saucepan. Ellen had taken it because it belonged to her mother. Martin had pointed out that they had bought it together in Worcester. Her mother had owned a similar one. He was right about the saucepan and wrong about almost everything surrounding it, a distinction he could not introduce into the original discussion.

He walked with two sticks, though he needed only one. The second gave the outing a professional character. At sixty-eight, he liked equipment that implied competence.

The road climbed above a reservoir toward an abandoned fire lookout. He intended to eat an apple there and return before the weather arrived.

Below a bend, a car had gone through young alders and stopped against a fir. At first he mistook the windshield’s pale crazing for reflected sky.

“Hello?” he called.

There was no answer.

Loose shale slid beneath his boots as he descended. He put down his sticks and went the last few feet on his hands.

A woman lay outside the open driver’s door. One shoe remained on her foot. The other stood beside a fern, as if placed there. Her gray jacket had a red lining.

He touched her shoulder.

“Can you hear me?”

His phone showed one bar, then none. The emergency call connected on his second attempt.

The dispatcher asked where he was. He gave the road name, the reservoir, the gate.

“Have you passed the lookout junction?”

“Not yet.”

She helped him find coordinates on his phone. He had owned it for four years without knowing it contained a compass.

Under her direction, he rolled the woman onto her back, checked for breathing, and began pressing on her chest.

His knees hurt on the stones. The jacket bunched beneath his wrists. He had a terrible wish that she would object.

The connection failed once. When the dispatcher called back, he was still pressing.

Eventually his arms would not straighten. He leaned forward again and managed only a shallow rocking movement.

“I can’t,” he said.

Her voice changed—not softened, exactly, but lowered into a register in which he was no longer required to prove anything.

Help was coming from the other side of a washout. Was he injured? Was there gasoline? Could he safely remain?

“Yes.”

She asked his name.

“Martin Vale.”

“Martin, keep your phone available.”

Afterward, the mountain resumed its sounds. Water worked beneath the road. A bird repeated a phrase that seemed to require an answer.

He put his fleece over the woman’s legs, then wondered whether he should have done that.

“I’m going to sit here,” he told her.

He found a flat place beside the fir. One bootlace had come loose. He tied it carefully.

For several minutes he said nothing.

Then he said, “I used to inspect bridges.”

He had not known he was going to begin.

“For the county. Culverts, mostly, by the end. People think a bridge is the part you drive over. Most of what matters is underneath.”

He waited with the residual politeness of conversation.

“I expect you know that.”

She might have inspected bridges herself. She might have despised men who explained bridges.

Through the station wagon’s rear window he saw a blanket, a box, and a bag of oranges. One orange had lodged behind the headrests. A dog lead lay on the seat.

He stood too quickly.

“Was there a dog?”

He searched around the car and called into the trees. Nothing moved except branches settling in the wind.

He phoned the dispatcher again. She said she would note it.

“They’ll look,” he told the woman.

His son had called the previous evening. That was partly why Martin had wanted to walk alone.

Daniel lived in Minneapolis with his husband and a child learning the cello. In the recordings, the bow seemed to be employed in a prolonged effort to open the instrument.

Daniel had asked whether Martin might consider moving closer.

“Not in with us,” he added.

“I didn’t imagine you meant in with you.”

“I’m just saying.”

“I heard you.”

Then each had waited for the other to become a different person.

Martin turned a fir cone between his fingers.

“My son thinks I’m lonely. It’s a reasonable theory.”

Sunlight moved down the opposite slope.

“When he was nine, we went camping. He wanted to sleep outside the tent. We waited until he fell asleep and carried him in. Next morning he thought he’d done it. Slept under the stars.”

Martin smiled.

“We never told him.”

He looked at the woman’s hand. A narrow silver ring encircled her middle finger. There was a dark mark beside her thumb, possibly ink.

“Perhaps we should have let him.”

He considered calling Daniel, but the necessary opening—I’ve found a dead woman—seemed too large to place without warning in his afternoon. Besides, he did not want to make her into news before help arrived.

The dispatcher called. The rescue team was approaching, more slowly than expected.

“If you’re cold, you can go up to the road. You don’t have to stay beside her.”

“I know.”

He did not know whether he had to stay. There was nobody to require it.

He ate half his apple and put the rest away. Eating felt wrong; throwing it into the woods felt worse.

When his mother was dying, she had repeatedly asked whether her car was locked. It had been sold eight months earlier. He kept explaining this with the strained patience he had mistaken for gentleness.

Finally Ellen said, “Just tell her you checked.”

He had disliked the suggestion. It seemed to concede too much.

On the last evening, he told his mother he had checked. The relief on her face made him leave the room.

He told the woman this, then regretted it.

“You don’t have to make anything of that.”

A gust moved through the fir. Something struck the car roof with a metallic tick.

He had begun to feel that his talking imposed a responsibility on her: to receive him, to absolve him. She had not agreed to any of it. Before this morning she had possessed a life in which Martin did not exist.

He fell silent.

A stone was wedged in the nearest tire. Grass lay flattened beneath the door. Where the car had struck the fir, pale wood showed through the bark.

In a few years he might walk this road and fail to find the place.

He tried imagining her approaching the bend, but could produce only the road and the movement of trees. There was no way to know what she had been thinking.

The cold reached his hands. He put them under his arms. His fleece remained over her legs.

From uphill came a sound like a dropped shovel.

Then someone called his name.

“Here!”

Three people descended through the alders. A man in an orange helmet slid the final yard and caught a tree. A woman asked Martin to step back.

He obeyed immediately.

They set down bags. The woman knelt where he had knelt. Someone asked when he had found the car.

He looked at his watch, though it could tell him nothing about the past.

“I called right away.”

“We’ll have that time.”

The man in the helmet offered a jacket.

“I have one.”

“We’ll get yours.”

Martin let himself be helped into it. The sleeves were too long.

Above them, a vehicle stopped. Someone called a question; someone answered. The place had become a work site, with tasks and people qualified to perform them.

Martin was grateful. He also felt, absurdly, dismissed from a job he had only just learned.

The kneeling woman stood and came over.

“Thank you for staying.”

He nodded. He wanted to mention the dog lead, but he already had. The orange behind the seat was not information they needed.

On the road, a deputy took his details. Martin spelled his surname twice and accepted a paper cup of water.

His phone showed a photograph Daniel had sent: the child holding his cello with stern disbelief. Behind him were a laundry basket and several small plants, some doing better than others.

Martin pressed the call button.

“Dad?”

He looked at the borrowed jacket and the dirt on his trousers.

“I’m here,” he said.

“I know. You called me.”

“Yes,” Martin said. “I did.”

Something moved at the other end, perhaps a chair.

“Hang on,” Daniel said. “Let me go somewhere I can hear you.”

Martin waited.
